Sequential ABC with random forests

Source: R/abc_sequential.R
abc_sequential.Rd

Narrows a wide prior towards the region that fits one observation, by rounds of simulation and ABC with random forests: the ABC sequential Monte Carlo with random forests (ABC-SMC-RF) of Dinh et al. (2025). The first round is a reference table drawn from the prior, as in abc_table(), and one forest per parameter as in abc_fit(). Each later round draws new parameters from the weighted parameters of the round before, perturbs them with a normal kernel of twice their weighted variance (Beaumont et al. 2009), draws again those outside the prior, simulates and fits new forests on the new simulations only. The variance of the kernel is that of the parameters of the round before weighted by their weights. The weights of a round are those the forests give to its simulations for the observation, times the prior and divided by the density of the proposal they were drawn from, so that the last round estimates the posterior under the prior and not under the proposal.

Usage

abc_sequential(
  prior,
  simulate,
  observed,
  n,
  rounds = 4,
  setup = NULL,
  summarise = function(sim, shared) summary_stats(sim, shared$tree),
  table = NULL,
  ntree = 500,
  min_node_size = 5,
  ncores = 1,
  seed = 1
)

# S3 method for class 'mc_abc_sequential'
predict(object, level = 0.9, round = length(object$rounds), ...)

# S3 method for class 'mc_abc_sequential'
plot(x, bins = 30, ...)

Arguments

prior

Named list with one numeric vector of length 2 per parameter, the lower and upper limits of its uniform prior, as in abc_table().

simulate, setup, summarise

Functions to simulate and summarise, as in abc_table(). setup is called once, with the seed that abc_table() would use, and what it returns is shared by all rounds.

observed

Named numeric vector of observed statistics, as from summary_stats(), or a data frame with one row.

n

Number of simulations per round. One whole number, 10 or more.

rounds

Number of rounds, the first from the prior. One whole number, 1 or more.

table

Optional reference table from the prior, as from abc_table() with the same prior, simulate, setup and summarise, used as the first round instead of new simulations. Its rows need not number n.

ntree, min_node_size, ncores

Passed to abc_fit().

seed

Integer that sets all the seeds. One finite whole number.

object

An mc_abc_sequential from abc_sequential().

level

Probability of the credible interval. One number greater than 0 and less than 1.

round

Round whose weighted parameters give the estimates. By default the last.

...

Not used.

x

An mc_abc_sequential from abc_sequential().

bins

Number of bins of the histograms. One whole number, 1 or more.

Value

An mc_abc_sequential: a list with rounds, one element per round with its table (an mc_abc_table), fit (an mc_abc_fit) and weights (a data frame with the parameters of the simulations kept by the fit and one column of normalised weights per parameter, named w_<parameter>); and parameters, statistics, prior and observed.

A data frame with one row per parameter: round, parameter, estimate (weighted median), low and high (the limits of the central credible interval), mean (weighted mean) and ess, the effective number of simulations behind the weights, 1 / sum(weights^2).

Details

The gain is in precision for the same number of simulations when the prior is wide and the posterior narrow, since later rounds simulate where the posterior is. The result belongs to one observation: a new observation needs new rounds, abc_recovery() and abc_calibrate() do not apply, and the coverage of the intervals can only be measured by repeating the whole procedure on pseudo-observations (data-raw/abc_sequential.R). As in abc_fit(), each parameter has its own forest and weights, so the proposal draws each parameter on its own and the correlation among parameters is not kept. The number of rounds is fixed: compare the posteriors of the last rounds, with predict() and its round, to see whether more would help.

The rounds can make the intervals too narrow. The posterior of a forest rests on few simulations, its effective number (ess of predict()), and its error of location follows the spread of the reference table rather than the width of the posterior. As the rounds concentrate the table, this error grows relative to the interval and builds up from round to round. In a toy model with a known posterior and one informative statistic (data-raw/abc_sequential.R), about 14 effective simulations per round brought the coverage of 90% intervals from 0.99 in the first round to 0.90 in the third and 0.85 in the fourth, while the same rounds with exact weights kept it at 0.92; wider kernels restored the coverage only by giving back the narrower intervals (data-raw/abc_sequential_diagnostics.R). In the community model of data-raw/abc_recovery.R, with 117 to 161 effective simulations, the coverage held. A warning is given when the last round has fewer than 50 effective simulations for some parameter; there, prefer fewer rounds and compare them.

References

Beaumont, M. A., Cornuet, J.-M., Marin, J.-M. & Robert, C. P. (2009). Adaptive approximate Bayesian computation. Biometrika 96: 983-990. doi:10.1093/biomet/asp052

Dinh, K. N., Liu, C., Xiang, Z., Liu, Z. & Tavaré, S. (2025). Approximate Bayesian computation sequential Monte Carlo via random forests. Statistics and Computing 35: 219. doi:10.1007/s11222-025-10748-x

Examples

# one statistic, the parameter plus noise, and a prior much wider than the posterior; with
# so few simulations the forests rest on a handful of them, hence the warning
toy <- function(scenario, shared) scenario$a + rnorm(1, 0, 0.1)
prior <- list(a = c(-10, 10))
seq_fit <- abc_sequential(prior, toy, observed = c(s = 2), n = 200, rounds = 3,
                          summarise = function(sim, shared) c(s = sim), ntree = 100)
#> abc_sequential() implements the method of:
#>   Dinh, K. N., Liu, C., Xiang, Z., Liu, Z., & Tavaré, S. (2025). Approximate Bayesian computation sequential Monte Carlo via random forests. Statistics and Computing, 35, 219. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-025-10748-x
#>   Beaumont, M. A., Cornuet, J.-M., Marin, J.-M., & Robert, C. P. (2009). Adaptive approximate Bayesian computation. Biometrika, 96, 983-990. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asp052
#>   Raynal, L., Marin, J.-M., Pudlo, P., Ribatet, M., Robert, C. P., & Estoup, A. (2019). ABC random forests for Bayesian parameter inference. Bioinformatics, 35, 1720-1728. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bty867
#> Please cite these papers together with comdynamite (citation("comdynamite")).
#> This message is shown once per session; options(comdynamite.cite = FALSE) turns it off.
#> Warning: abc_sequential(): Fewer than 50 effective simulations in the last round for a; the intervals may be too narrow. Compare the rounds with predict(round = ).
seq_fit
#> Sequential ABC with random forests: 3 rounds, 600 simulations used
#> Parameters: a 
#> Statistics: 1 
#>  parameter estimate  low high  ess
#>          a     1.94 1.88 2.05 5.21
#> Effective simulations per round:
#>           a
#> round 1 5.9
#> round 2 3.7
#> round 3 5.2
predict(seq_fit, round = 1)
#>   round parameter estimate     low     high     mean      ess
#> 1     1         a 1.975219 1.91424 2.106069 1.992312 5.921633
